corpus.title: Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
corpus.signal_text:
Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.

Addis Ababa tells a different story, arguing that armed rebels ordered an “all-out offensive” against federal positions in the Afar and Amhara regions as well as seized three airports in nearby Tigray. “The TPLF politico-military leadership has obviously taken irresponsibility to new heights,” Getachew Reda, an advisor to Abiy and a former TPLF official, wrote on social media.

corpus.title: After seizing Tigray airports, TPLF announces ‘defensive war’ against Ethiopian govt
corpus.signal_text:
After seizing Tigray airports, TPLF announces ‘defensive war’ against Ethiopian govt          
        The confrontation between the Tigray regional government and the Ethiopian federal government entered a new phase on Wednesday when Tigrayan forces seized control of the Mekelle, Axum and Shire airports.
Clashes broke out at several locations in the restive northern state, the site of a two-year civil war that concluded in 2022, and in the neighboring Afar region — a development that has pushed the Ethiopian conflict back toward open warfare, four years after the signing of the Pretoria Agreement that ended the previous war between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and federal forces.
A source in the Tigray regional administration told Mada Masr that the seizure of the airports was part of a military redeployment that began in the early hours of Wednesday, with Tigrayan forces using the airports as facilities of operational importance amid the expanding scope of the fighting.
In the wake of the TPLF takeover, Ethiopian Airlines announced the suspension of flights to the three airports due to the “current situation” in the Tigray region.
A Tigrayan military source noted that Wednesday’s developments followed months of troop buildup and limited skirmishes along the front lines, describing Wednesday’s events as a shift from a phase of mutual pressure to direct confrontation. He added that Tigrayan forces view federal movements as an attempt to alter the military landscape established since the Pretoria Agreement and believe that seizing certain vital sites could prevent federal forces from utilizing the region’s civilian and military infrastructure during ongoing operations.
The federal government framed Wednesday’s events differently. A former security source in Addis Ababa described the movements by the TPLF as a “full-scale attack” on government positions in Afar and Amhara.
While seizing airports does not in itself decide the outcome of the battle, it signals a shift in the nature of operations, a security source in Addis Ababa told Mada Masr. Mekelle serves as the region’s political and administrative hub, while the airports at Axum and Shire provide crucial links to northern and western Tigray. Consequently, placing airports under the control of regional forces strains the federal government’s ability to manage its presence within the region and gives Tigrayan forces a strategic advantage in any future negotiations, the source said.

corpus.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
corpus.signal_text:
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.
About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.
On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.
The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.
Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.
A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”
The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.
The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.
In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.
